title: Three Outputs of Truly Great Teachers
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart borrows Jim Collins' three markers of organizational greatness from Good to Great — superior results, distinctive impact, lasting endurance — and applies them to individual teachers. Superior results, he argues, means efficient, intelligent production of measurable student growth given real constraints, not raw effort. Distinctive impact is tested by a thought experiment: if you vanished tomorrow, would there be a "gaping hole" no other teacher could fill in quite the same way, which he illustrates with named colleagues whose irreplaceability comes from being fully themselves rather than interchangeable. Lasting endurance is the hardest of the three in a culture obsessed with instant wins, since real greatness is proven only across the ebb and flow of hard years and easy years, not by a single award or bestseller. The article closes with reassurance rather than pressure: readers wondering whether they're great are probably already on the way, because time — not a single dramatic outcome — is what actually confers it.
points: Translates a business framework (Collins' Good to Great) directly onto individual teaching practice rather than school-level organizational change, making it usable by a single classroom teacher.
Defines "distinctive impact" via a concrete self-test — would there be a "gaping hole" if I left tomorrow? — rather than a vague appeal to being special.
Explicitly warns against ego-driven readings of distinctive impact, framing it as "becoming more who we are" rather than pride-seeking.
Positions "lasting endurance" as the counter-cultural marker of greatness, arguing against the impulse to chase awards or single dramatic wins as proof of quality.
quotes: No living person has thought more about the word "great" than Jim Collins has in his long and focused career. If you're a teacher in search of surprising insights into both your career and your life, you could do a lot worse than picking up Collins' Good to Great.
For me as an individual teacher, superior results look like efficiently and intelligently producing as much growth in my students as I can, given my constraints.
Distinctive impact means that, were we to vanish tomorrow, there'd be a "gaping hole" that could not be easily filled by any other teacher. If we went away, would we be missed — and why?
Ours is a now-now–NOW culture; we want overnight successes and wild trajectories. But you can't be great, according to Collins, if you're a flash in the pan.

Time, inevitably, brings setbacks. It brings easy years and hard years; seasons of white-hot passion and seasons of ennui. Producing superior results and having distinctive impact in the ebb and flow of years and decades…that's what makes an educator truly great.
